headline: Lenoir County commissioners approve stop sign resolution, strategic planning contract
hook: A new all-way stop is coming to Smith-Grady and Burncoat roads. Here is what else commissioners approved.
next_step: Add dollar amounts, locations and vote details if available.
body: Lenoir County commissioners approved an all-way stop at Smith-Grady Road and Burncoat Road on Tuesday, along with contracts, grants, appointments and several budget-related items during their regular meeting. The board also welcomed a new finance officer, recognized the retirement of a longtime sheriff's office employee, honored the late Eleanor Mills Harvey and proclaimed Constitution Week in Lenoir County. Commissioners approved the all-way stop after a split discussion over whether additional four-way stops improve safety or slow traffic and commerce across the county. The resolution passed 4-2, with Commissioners June Cummings and Eric Rouse voting against it. Commissioner Keith King was absent. NCDOT's Chris Smith said the intersection has a history of serious crashes. According to the agenda packet, NCDOT reported 12 crashes, 20 injuries and one death during a 10-year review period from Nov. 1, 2015, to Oct. 31, 2025. Smith said three additional crashes occurred after previous safety improvements, bringing the reviewed total to 14 angle crashes, one left-turn crash from a different roadway, 12 injury crashes, one death and 23 injuries. Smith said the state had already tried lower-cost safety improvements, including larger signs, warning signs, bright strips and sign relocations. He said a roundabout was reviewed but estimated to cost $1.5 million to $3 million. "Based on crash history, HSIP findings, sight-distance limitations and the persistence of crashes even after improvements, the division continues to recommend installing an all-way stop at this intersection," Smith said. Rouse, who serves on the Lenoir County Transportation Committee, said the committee did not recommend the proposal. He said residents have complained about the number of four-way stops on roads such as N.C. 55 and N.C. 903, and he said navigation apps are pushing drivers onto secondary roads. "Any loss of life is tragic, any accident is tragic, but we can't regulate ourselves out of people not paying attention," Rouse said. Commissioner Mac Daughety disagreed, saying the Smith-Grady and Burncoat intersection is not a major commercial corridor. He said residents in that area requested the all-way stop because of crashes and speeding traffic. "The citizens want this," Daughety said. "It is seldom that you find citizens that want a four-way. They requested this four-way because they are desperate to slow down the crashes and the traffic that is coming through their neighborhood." Before the vote, Chair Linda Rouse Sutton clarified that the board was voting to authorize the all-way stop, despite the Transportation Committee's unfavorable recommendation. The board also approved setting a public hearing for Sept. 21 on a special use permit request for a campground on parcel 8670 and a rezoning request to change parcel 18387 from agriculture/rural to commercial. Commissioners granted Duke Energy a utility easement across county-owned property to provide residential electric service to 146 Futrell Lane. Assistant County Manager Adam Short said the property owner had been informed of floodplain restrictions and other requirements for future residential use. The board approved the sheriff's office request to purchase 10 Dell laptops for patrol vehicles at a cost of $31,832. Sheriff Jackie Rogers said the laptops are needed for new deputies and are expected to be reimbursed once state allocation funds are received. Commissioners also authorized a contract of up to $20,000 with Allies4Outcomes for temporary intensive support social work services. County Manager Michael James said the contract will help cover after-hours emergency calls and adult services work while the Department of Social Services manages staffing shortages and employee leave. "This contract will help us assist staff for a 30-day period until that staffing stabilizes," James said. The board approved a $58,000 agreement with Hayes Group Consulting for strategic planning services tied to the county's 2030 strategic plan. James said the county's current plan, built in 2020, needs a broader update that includes stakeholder interviews, department head feedback and long-term planning for the next four fiscal years. "We wanted to do kind of a larger, robust planning process to prepare for the next four fiscal years," James said. Commissioners approved an agreement of up to $92,000 with the 9th Judicial District Adult Accountability and Recovery Court and the North Carolina Administrative Office of the Courts. Audra Haddad said the one-year contract renews an arrangement in place since 2022 and supports the adult accountability and recovery court case coordinator position through grant funding. Sutton praised the recovery court program, calling it a model for others. "A lot of folks may not realize that what we have got is a model program here in Lenoir County," Sutton said. The board also approved the fiscal year 2027 Rural Operating Assistance Program grant application for transit services totaling $191,568. The funding includes $83,236 for elderly and disabled transportation assistance, $14,637 for employment transportation and $93,695 for rural general public transportation. Under appointments, commissioners approved second-reading appointments to the Juvenile Crime Prevention Council for Cleveland Lovick, June Cummings, Jeffrey Cannon, Christie Hale, Jessica Drennan, Laura Beth Blalock and Suzanne Newsome. Earlier in the meeting, James introduced Blake Batchelor as Lenoir County's new finance officer. Batchelor previously served as finance director for Jones County government and has experience with the town of Trenton. "I've been very impressed so far with everybody I've met throughout the county and all the projects you have going on," Batchelor said. The board also recognized Major Shawn Howard on his retirement from the Lenoir County Sheriff's Office. Howard thanked current and former sheriffs, county officials and his family, and reflected on a law enforcement career that began in 1999. "When I first started this profession I never imagined that this job would have carried me the places that it carried me and enabled me to gain the experiences that I've been able to experience along this journey," Howard said. Commissioner Preston Harris read proclamations honoring Harvey and recognizing Constitution Week. Harvey, who died June 19 at age 75, was remembered for her work in education, service through Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. and influence on generations of students. Her husband, Nicholas Harvey Sr., and son, Nicholas Harvey II, accepted the honor. "Every time someone shares an experience with Mom, that sustains our family," Nicholas Harvey II said. Theresa Hardy and Glenda Alcock of the Mosley-Bright Chapter of the National Society Daughters of the American Revolution accepted the Constitution Week proclamation. The week will be observed Sept. 17-23, with a bell-ringing event scheduled for 4 p.m. Sept. 17 at Harmony Hall. Commissioners approved the consent agenda, which included minutes from the Aug. 17 meeting, the Harvey and Constitution Week proclamations, authorization of Howard's retirement badge and service weapon, tax relief applications, a $10 fee for county-sponsored rabies vaccination clinics, a position and pay classification plan amendment, a $4,491.77 purchase order to Whaley Food Service, several budget amendments and health department service agreements. The board later voted to enter closed session to consult with an attorney and discuss a personnel matter.

headline: Jones County seeks more foster families to help children remain close to home
hook: Jones County says it needs more foster families so children can stay closer to home.
next_step: Confirm contact information and avoid identifying children.
body: Jones County officials are seeking additional foster families to provide temporary, stable homes for children who cannot safely remain with their biological families. Six children from Jones County are currently in foster care, while fewer than 10 licensed foster homes are available within the county, according to Jones County Department of Social Services Director Dr. Chris Meadows. “We are grateful for these foster parents and appreciate their continued commitment to children,” Meadows said. The limited number of licensed homes can make it difficult to place children within Jones County. When a local placement is unavailable, children may experience additional disruption by being placed outside their community. “When a child is separated from their home and set to enter foster care, trauma often occurs,” Meadows said. “A foster family in Jones County will offer the child the opportunity to remain close to home, which causes less of a disruption in their surroundings and routines.” Local placements can allow children to remain in the same school and maintain connections with teachers, friends and other community members. They can also help children remain closer to their biological families while social workers and families work toward reunification. “An increase in foster families in Jones will enable children to remain familiar with their community and limit disruption,” Meadows said. “Having more foster families in Jones County would be incredible and aid immensely in the ultimate goal of family reunification.” Prospective foster parents do not have to be married, wealthy or homeowners. Single adults who are at least 21 years old may qualify, and foster parents may live in rented homes. The primary considerations are financial stability and the ability to provide a safe, supportive environment for a child. “One of the greatest challenges in recruiting foster families is the misconceptions surrounding foster care,” Meadows said. “Many people believe that they must own a home, be married and have a high income. However, this is not the case.” Applicants must complete background checks and meet North Carolina’s foster home licensing requirements. The process includes orientation, pre-service training, a home inspection and a safety assessment. Training helps prospective foster parents understand childhood trauma, the effects of separation from biological parents and the behaviors and needs children may have after entering foster care. Licensed foster parents also receive continued training and support. Prior parenting experience is not required. “Some also think that they need to have a great deal of parenting experience, but with consistent training and guidance, prospective foster parents will gain these skills and more,” Meadows said. Another misconception is that foster parents are expected to adopt the children placed in their homes. Foster care is generally intended to be temporary, with reunification remaining the primary goal when it can be accomplished safely. “The primary goal of foster parenting is to provide a temporary, safe location for the children until reunification with the family can be achieved,” Meadows said. Foster parents receive financial reimbursement to help cover the costs of caring for a child. The reimbursement is not intended to serve as a primary source of income, but foster parents are not expected to personally absorb all expenses related to the child’s care. Foster families also work with a team that may include social workers, teachers, counselors, therapists, attorneys and members of the child’s biological family when appropriate. Jones County Consolidated Health and Human Services supports the Community Closet, which collects donated clothing and provides it to county residents at no cost. The closet is also available as a resource for foster families who need children’s clothing. Residents who are not prepared to become licensed foster parents may still assist by supporting existing foster families or working with organizations serving children and their families. Those interested in becoming foster parents or learning more may call the Jones County Department of Social Services at 252-448-2581 or visit the department at 418 N.C. 58 North, Unit D, in Trenton.

headline: Jones County Spotlight: Halle Powell uses dance to serve seniors across North Carolina
hook: At 19, Halle Powell has turned dance into a statewide service mission.
next_step: Request or select strong submitted photos.
body: COMFORT - At 19, Halle Powell is already blending her love of dance, service and senior care into a statewide mission. Powell, a Jones County native from Comfort, is the founder of The Senior Shuffle Project, a nonprofit that provides seated dance classes for seniors in eldercare communities. The classes are offered both in person and virtually, giving seniors a way to stay active, build community and enjoy movement in a safe, accessible way. Powell said she first began serving in senior living communities at age 14 and created The Senior Shuffle Project when she was 16. The idea grew from time spent visiting eldercare centers, where she noticed many residents often remained isolated in their rooms. “I saw a gap in the senior community that I had the ability to fill,” Powell said. Her program uses seated dance, TapFit silicone tap shoes that slide over regular shoes and tambourines for seniors with limited mobility. Powell said seated dance can support physical, mental and emotional health while giving residents a shared activity to enjoy. The project has reached more than 300 people through in-person classes, and Powell said virtual classes through YouTube have reached all 100 North Carolina counties. In June, she hosted Senior Shuffle Day across the state, including an in-person event at the Trenton Senior Center with 34 seniors. Powell recently partnered with Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina and received a $3,000 grant to purchase 2,400 tambourines for senior facilities across the state. She also wrote letters to eldercare communities in nearly every county and is working to distribute the instruments to support virtual classes. Among her most meaningful moments was seeing a stroke survivor tap his foot during one of her classes. “He yelled, ‘look everybody, my foot, it’s moving,’” Powell said. “To watch it come to life in person will always be the most rewarding moment of The Senior Shuffle Project.” Powell is a graduate of Lenoir County Early College, where she earned two associate degrees. She is now a freshman at UNC-Chapel Hill, majoring in business administration with a concentration in business of health and minoring in social work. She is a direct admit to the Kenan-Flagler Business School. In addition to her nonprofit work, Powell is a dancer and competitor in the Miss America Opportunity. She has held the titles of Miss Wendell’s Teen and Miss Cleveland, and recently competed for Miss North Carolina. She said pageantry has helped her grow as a speaker, servant leader and advocate. Powell said community service gives her a chance to be part of something bigger than herself. “It was never about me; it was always about them,” Powell said. “I hope they see the value in seniors and understand that they deserve to be able to keep their bodies moving.” Looking ahead, Powell hopes to graduate from UNC-Chapel Hill debt-free and return to eastern North Carolina to continue serving seniors in eldercare. She said she can see herself working in management at an eldercare facility or with a company that provides senior care. Powell said Jones County remains central to who she is and what she hopes to accomplish. “I love where I live,” Powell said. “I may wear the names of other places on a sash across my chest, but every time I step on stage or in an interview room, I do it with Jones County on my mind and in my heart.” People can support The Senior Shuffle Project by sharing its website, subscribing to its YouTube channel or selecting the nonprofit for Walmart round-up donations. The project’s website is seniorshuffleproject.wixsite.com/official, and its YouTube channel is @theseniorshuffleproject.

headline: Back-to-School with Neuse Regional Libraries
hook: As the summer winds down and kids across our region head back to school, Neuse Regional Libraries staff are reflecting on what a busy summer it has been. Over the six weeks of the Unearth a Story Summer Reading Program, 785 participants (ages 0-18) read 164,760 minutes.

body: By Amber Hargett, Head of Youth Services As the summer winds down and kids across our region head back to school, Neuse Regional Libraries staff are reflecting on what a busy summer it has been. Over the six weeks of the Unearth a Story Summer Reading Program, 785 participants (ages 0-18) read 164,760 minutes. Across that same age range, the Libraries offered 160 programs with 3,340 in attendance. Little ones stomped and roared like dinosaurs, while enjoying well-loved songs and picture books. School aged participants designed paleontologist hats and baked dinosaur-shaped pizza quesadillas, while the teens survived the lost expedition escape room and crafted resin amber fossil bracelets, just to name a few of the activities participants enjoyed this summer. Now it is time to return to school and get back to a routine including regular visits to your local library. The Neuse Regional Libraries are excited to offer a weekly series of afterschool programs for school age participants. Afterschool Adventures combines some of our most popular programs with a different monthly theme. Throughout the month, participants will enjoy messy art, edible experiments, crafternoon creation sessions, game nights, and much more. Afterschool Adventures kicks off the week of September 14 at the following Neuse Regional Library locations: Comfort Public Library - Every 3rd Thursday at 5:30pm Greene County Public Library - Mondays at 4:00 p.m. Kinston-Lenoir County Public Library - Thursdays at 4:30 p.m. La Grange Public Library- Tuesdays at 4:00 p.m. Maysville Public Library - Thursdays at 4:30 p.m. Pink Hill Public Library - Tuesdays at 4:30 p.m. Pollocksville Public Library - Tuesdays at 4:00 p.m. Trenton Public Library - Thursdays at 4:00 p.m. Our theme for the month of September is “ It’s Carnival Time!” and participants will enjoy a range of activities from pendulum painting to decorating chocolate covered caramel apple slices to testing balloon rockets and carnival style games. Stop by your local Neuse Regional Library to try the spinning wheel challenge and stay for circus bingo. It is a great time to catch up with old friends and make some new ones as we kick off Afterschool Adventures. If you have any questions about Afterschool Adventures or other Neuse Regional Libraries’ programs, please feel free to contact the Head of Youth Services at 252-527-7066, ext. 125 or via email at ahargett@neuselibrary.org .

body: Kenneth “Ken” Graham Crossno, 74, of Kinston, NC, passed away unexpectedly on September 3, 2026, leaving behind a lifetime of love, laughter, and stories his family and friends will carry forever. The youngest of three sons, Ken was born on December 30, 1951, in Warsaw, North Carolina to a Methodist minister and a mother he adored. As a young boy, he moved to Enfield, NC, which he considered his hometown. He described his growing up there as a magical childhood and formed many friendships that lasted a lifetime. He later graduated from Atlantic Christian College and built a career first in banking and later in social services. He was the beloved husband of 49 years to Carol Dobey Crossno, a devoted father to his two daughters, and a cherished “Paw Paw” to his grandchildren. Family was the center of his world, and he took deep pride and joy in watching his daughters and grandchildren grow. He cherished his faithful companion, his dog Boo, and found joy in The Beatles, Duke basketball, classic horror films, and the spirit of Halloween. Those who knew Ken will remember his quick wit, sharp humor, and unmatched way with words — heartfelt, hilarious, and uniquely Ken. He had a gift for making people laugh, making them think, and leaving them with a story worth remembering. Ken is survived by his wife, Carol Crossno of Kinston, NC; daughters Candace Friedman (David Friedman) of Winston-Salem, NC, and Lauren Watkins (Brandon Landreth) of Clayton, NC; grandchildren Grace, Colin, Sullivan, and Piper; brother John Crossno (Kimla Crossno); sister-in-law Barbie Ferguson (Geoff Ferguson); as well as cousins, nieces, and nephews who he loved dearly. He was preceded in death by his parents, Reverend Leon and Katherine Crossno, and his brother, Bobby Crossno. Ken’s laughter, wit, and unmistakable personality will live on in the hearts of all who knew and loved him. A celebration of life will be held Saturday, September 12, with visitation at 1 PM and a service at 2 PM, both at Howard-Carter Funeral Home, 1608 W Vernon Avenue, Kinston, NC 28504 with Pastor Allen Stocks officiating. headline: John Hood: Carolina job growth beats national trend
hook: According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, North Carolina experienced no net job growth in July. Indeed, employers as a whole reported 3,000 fewer people on the payroll in July than in May.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: RALEIGH — According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, North Carolina experienced no net job growth in July. Indeed, employers as a whole reported 3,000 fewer people on the payroll in July than in May. Year-to-year, our state’s job-growth rate was just 1%. While employment figures over the 2021-24 period were skewed by COVID, North Carolina routinely experienced 1.5% to 2% annual growth in employment before the pandemic. Should we be worried about this? It depends on how you define the subject of that question. If by “we” you mean Americans as a whole, I’d say yes. To be sure, unemployment rates remain low by historical standards. Our population is aging, with more people choosing to retire rather than remain in the labor force. And since the start of 2025, the Trump administration’s tougher approach to immigration enforcement has both reduced inflows of foreign workers and motivated some illegal residents to “self-deport,” in both cases reducing the number of new positions required each month to absorb job seekers. Partly as a result of these factors, America’s labor force participation rate has shrinking for the better part of a year. But less-robust job growth also translates into less-robust economic growth. Even in our age of automation and artificial intelligence, enterprises still need people to deliver the goods and services customers demand (including all those retirees!) The reason North Carolina leaders, in particular, ought not panic is that these employment trends are general, not particular. Even at 1% year-to-year growth, our job-creation rate exceeds that of most other states and far exceeds the national average of 0.2%. Over the longer term, mid-2016 to mid-2026, North Carolina posted a 17.3% increase in employment, larger than the national average of 9.9% and the employment gains of our neighboring states of South Carolina (17%), Tennessee (13.7%), Georgia (13.6%), and Virginia (8%). Moreover, while the constant churn of heightened competition, technological innovations, and shifting consumer preferences have resulted in the elimination of some well-paying jobs across our state, other positions have been created. Please note that the statistics I cited earlier were net employment changes. Every week, thousands of preexisting jobs disappear. During the fourth quarter of 2025, in fact, North Carolina companies eliminated more than 400,000 positions! Why don’t we recall that period as some sort of economic Armageddon? Because during those same three months, companies added nearly 450,000 new positions. The net effect wasn’t just more employment. North Carolinians as a whole have enjoyed income gains , not income losses. From the first quarter of 2016 to the first quarter of 2026, for example, the average weekly wage rose by 18% after adjusting for inflation. We also experienced a 20% real gain in personal income per North Carolinian over the past decade, again beating the national average and most of our neighbors. I don’t discount the disappointment and dismay experienced by those whose jobs go away. Over the years, I had friends and family members displaced by the economic churn I’m describing here. They’ve had to refocus, reskill, and in some cases relocate. Public policy has a role to play, from financing education and training programs to reforming regulations that inhibit entering new occupations, building new enterprises, and creating new jobs. What public policy cannot do is arrest such changes in labor markets or the broader economy, Attempts to do so invariably hurt far more than they help. During North Carolina’s first century as a state, the vast majority of its residents worked on farms. It wasn’t until the early 20th century that agricultural jobs fell below 50% of total employment. Around 1950, manufacturing surpassed agriculture as the largest employment sector and rose to a high point of about 35% by 1970. Employment in services overtook manufacturing in 1970 and now accounts for most North Carolina jobs. Specific figures and time periods vary, but other states — and industrialized countries — have exhibited essentially the same trend. North Carolina has handled these changes better than most. John Hood is a John Locke Foundation board member. His books Mountain Folk, Forest Folk, and Water Folk combine epic fantasy with American history (FolkloreCycle.com).

Legislation of the Week Senate Bill 889– Property Tax Reappraisal Moratorium Sponsored by Senators Phil Berger, Brent Jackson, and Steve Jarvis Senate Bill 889, the Property Tax Reappraisal Moratorium, provides temporary relief for property owners in certain North Carolina counties by delaying the implementation of new property values resulting from 2026 reappraisals. The legislation requires qualifying counties that conducted a reappraisal effective January 1, 2026, to use their previous schedule of property values for the 2026-2027 tax year. The new 2026 property values will instead take effect beginning with the 2027-2028 tax year. Senator Jackson served as a primary sponsor of the legislation, which passed the General Assembly and was signed into law on June 19, 2026, becoming Session Law 2026-8. Property reappraisals can result in significant changes to assessed values for homeowners, farmers and businesses. Senate Bill 889 gives affected property owners additional time before newly appraised values are used for property tax purposes while maintaining the state's regular reappraisal process moving forward. Read More Ever Wonder What Happens When the Governor Vetoes a Bill? After a bill passes the General Assembly and is presented to the Governor, the Governor can sign it into law, allow it to become law without a signature, or veto it. When a bill is vetoed, it is returned to the chamber where it originated along with the Governor’s objections. Lawmakers then have the opportunity to reconsider the bill and attempt to override the veto. In North Carolina, overriding a veto requires a three-fifths vote of the members present and voting in both the House and Senate. If both chambers reach that threshold, the bill becomes law despite the Governor’s veto. So, a Governor’s veto does not necessarily mean the end of a bill—the General Assembly still has an opportunity to give it the final word. The first major group, known as the Argyll Colony, arrived in 1739. About 350 men, women and children from the Scottish Highlands settled along the Cape Fear River. Larger waves followed during the decades leading up to the American Revolution, with many families seeking affordable land and greater economic opportunity. The Upper Cape Fear eventually became the largest concentration of Highland Scots in America. Their settlements spread through areas that today include Bladen and Sampson counties, along with Cumberland, Harnett, Hoke, Moore, Richmond, Robeson, Scotland and Anson counties. By the time of the Revolution, as many as 10,000 Highland Scots may have lived along the Cape Fear and its tributaries. Many became farmers or entered the naval stores industry, using the region's abundant pine forests to produce tar, pitch and turpentine. These products were transported down the Cape Fear River to Wilmington and became an important part of North Carolina's early economy. The Highland Scots helped shape communities throughout southeastern North Carolina, and their influence remains an important part of the region's heritage nearly three centuries later. body: In death as in life, Thomas Walter Rouse, 69, answered the call of his Master, took His hand, and followed where He led. Entering into the joy of his salvation, new life for Thomas began on Sunday, September 6, 2026. Thomas was born in Lenoir County to the late J.B. and Shirley Rouse on August 29, 1957. For Thomas, faith was never confined to Sunday morning. It was the foundation upon which he built his life and the testimony that shaped everything he did. Whether behind the wheel of a UPS truck, driving a church bus filled with children, leading a hymn, comforting a grieving family, sitting in a tree stand, fishing from a boat, or simply talking with a friend, Thomas sought to live in a way that reflected the Lord he loved and faithfully served. Faith was not something Thomas merely professed; it was something he practiced. Each day began in Scripture and prayer, and his last conversation of each day was with his Lord. He possessed a gentleness that seemed to flow naturally from that relationship. Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in love, Thomas tried to see in every person someone created and loved by God. It was exceedingly rare, if ever, to hear Thomas speak a harsh word about another person. When others might have complained, criticized, or held a grudge, Thomas was more likely to carry the matter to God in prayer. And when he told someone that he would pray for them, those were not empty words. Oftentimes, he would pray right then and there with them. Even in circumstances that were far removed from his own personal experience, Thomas had a remarkable gift of empathy that allowed him to provide immeasurable comfort. Listening to Thomas pray revealed that he did not speak to a distant God, but to One he knew. His prayers had the warmth and familiarity of a conversation with an old and trusted friend. The gifts Thomas possessed were never his alone. They were gifts from God, and he believed they were meant to be returned to God in service. Among those gifts was a beautiful tenor voice, which he used to faithfully sing in the church choir, to lead singing during Sunday school and Wednesday night services, and to sing for many grieving families during funeral services. As long as the church operated bus routes for Sunday services, Thomas faithfully drove one, making certain that children who might otherwise have had no way to attend church were given the opportunity to come, to be welcomed, and to hear about the love of Christ. Thomas carried that same spirit into his work. During his more than thirty years with UPS, strangers along his route had a way of becoming customers, and customers had a way of becoming friends. He quickly learned the addresses along his route and, more importantly, the people who lived there. He knew their families, their joys, their struggles, and the things that mattered to them. He genuinely cared about people, and no job title could contain the ministry that naturally grew from the way he treated them. Following his retirement from UPS, Thomas worked in landscaping for several years before discovering another place of ministry in his work with Rouse Funeral Home. There, his deep work ethic was matched by even deeper compassion. He understood that the people he encountered were often living through some of the most difficult days of their lives, and he served them with patience, tenderness, dignity, and genuine concern. Thomas also knew how to enjoy the life God had given him. An avid hunter and fisherman, he loved the outdoors. Climbing up in a tree stand, cutting grass on his tractor with the bushhog, and spending time in his cabin were among the many things that brought him joy. A trip to the mountains of North Carolina was always welcome, whether it was riding the length of the parkway, enjoying the views at the Linn Cove Viaduct, and camping on Mt. Mitchell or staying in a hotel in Boone and visiting the Christian Bookstore. With an excellent sense of humor, he could laugh, tell a story, enjoy good company, and find delight in the people and places he loved. Of all the earthly blessings entrusted to Thomas, however, none was more precious to him than his family. A fierce protector, he was loving, fair, faithful, and constant. He was intentional in spending time with each one of them, and their home was the neighborhood spot for all friends to gather. Always up for a good time, family gatherings brought him great joy. In quiet time at home, he loved watching Carolina basketball and the old television shows, especially Bonanza, Gunsmoke, and The Andy Griffith Show. A service of love and remembrance will be held at 11:00 a.m. on Thursday, September 10, 2026 at Faith Free Will Baptist Church with Pastor Christian Powell and Pastor Dann Patrick officiating. Thomas’s family will receive friends prior to the service, beginning at 9:30 a.m. A graveside committal will follow the service at Fairview Cemetery in La Grange. Thomas is survived by his wife of forty-seven years, Janice Rouse; children, Brandon Rouse and wife Lauren and Melissa Baker and husband Chad; grandchildren, Rebecca Rouse, Andrew Rouse, Kamryn Rouse, Mikah Rouse, and Brody Rouse; grand-dog, Dash Baker; sister, Melony Brown and husband Larry; and nephews, Matthew Brown and wife Jessica, and Christopher Brown and wife Makayla. Online condolences may be expressed at www.rousefh.com. Flowers are welcome, or memorial contributions may be made to Faith Free Will Baptist Church, 1200 West Grantham Street, Goldsboro, NC 27530. Arrangements are entrusted to Rouse Funeral Home, La Grange.

body: Cary, Greensboro, Rocky Mount and Zebulon are among the larger governments being added to a state assistance list based on fiscal 2025 audits. RALEIGH — North Carolina’s Local Government Commission is changing how it identifies financially troubled local governments, applying its oversight criteria to larger municipalities that historically may have been left off the state’s assistance list. Cary, Greensboro, Rocky Mount and Zebulon are among the larger government units being placed on the commission’s updated Unit Assistance List based on fiscal 2025 audit reports, the Department of State Treasurer announced Friday. The list is used to identify counties, municipalities, utility authorities and other local-government units that may require additional monitoring or financial-management assistance. Historically, larger governments that met the list’s criteria were not always included when commission staff determined that those governments had sufficient internal resources to address their problems. The commission said it is ending that distinction and applying the standards more consistently regardless of a government’s size. “Financial concerns should be taken seriously regardless of the size of the local government,” State Treasurer Brad Briner said. The decision has statewide oversight implications because the Local Government Commission monitors the financial condition of more than 1,100 local-government units. Briner chairs the commission, which is staffed by the Department of State Treasurer. Rocky Mount remains under enhanced monitoring as state staff work with municipal officials to address financial and operational concerns, according to the department. The Unit Assistance List helps the commission determine how to allocate its monitoring and assistance resources. The fall 2025 list, which was based on fiscal 2024 audits, included 146 counties, municipalities and utility authorities or districts. The complete September 2026 list will be published after all affected governments have been notified. Placement on the list signals that a government meets financial or operational criteria requiring additional attention. The department’s announcement did not say that the commission had assumed control of any of the four governments identified in the release. Stein met with aspiring and beginning teachers at the UNCG School of Education following enactment of the state’s first complete budget in more than two years. headline: Audit finds digital lottery games drive sales as education share fall
hook: A state audit found that digital instant games now account for about 40% of North Carolina lottery sales as the share transferred to education has fallen.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: Digital instant games generated $2.6 billion in fiscal 2025, but their higher prize payouts contributed to a decline in the percentage of lottery sales transferred to education. RALEIGH — Digital instant games have helped drive a sharp increase in North Carolina Education Lottery sales while reducing the percentage of sales transferred to education, according to a state performance audit released Tuesday. Lottery sales increased 51% in two years, rising from $4.3 billion in fiscal 2023 to $6.6 billion in fiscal 2025, the North Carolina Office of the State Auditor reported. During the same period, the percentage of sales transferred to the state Education Lottery Fund fell from 23% to 16%. The dollar amount transferred increased from $1.02 billion in fiscal 2023 to $1.09 billion in fiscal 2024 before declining to $1.08 billion in fiscal 2025. The lottery has distributed $12.3 billion to education programs since its inception, according to the audit. Auditors attributed much of the change to the rapid growth of digital instant games, which resemble slot-machine games and carry an approximate prize payout rate of 87%. Digital instant-game sales grew from zero in fiscal 2023 to $2.6 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for about 40% of all lottery sales. Prize expenses increased from 66% to 76% of gross sales as digital games expanded, traditional lottery-product sales declined and the lottery offered more games with higher payout rates. North Carolina law sets a target of transferring approximately 38% of lottery revenue to education “to the extent practicable,” but the target is not mandatory. The auditor’s office said state lottery laws were not developed with digital instant games in mind. Auditors recommended that the lottery work with the General Assembly to clarify its primary policy objective. Lawmakers could direct the lottery to prioritize the total amount transferred to education, establish a minimum transfer percentage or balance both goals through a defined policy framework. Lottery officials agreed to review the findings with the North Carolina State Lottery Commission and meet with legislative leaders about possible changes. The auditor’s office disclosed that the state auditor appoints one member of the Lottery Commission. headline: Op-ed: More Housing Options Offer More Resources for NC Families
hook: by Wadeyn Norris, State Chairman of the NC Federation of College Republicans In much of the state, fewer than 1% of for-sale homes are available at any given time — far below the 2–3% economists consider a healthy market. In the Triangle and Charlotte, where employers keep adding jobs faster than builders can add roofs, the math simply doesn't work for a growing share of families.

approved_script_lines: North Carolina families are facing a housing shortage. In much of the state, fewer than 1% of homes are available for sale at any given time—well below what economists consider a healthy market.
In this op-ed, Wadeyn Norris argues that single-family rental homes can provide an immediate option while zoning reforms and new construction move forward.

These homes can offer families more space, a yard and access to preferred school districts—without requiring a large down payment or long-term mortgage commitment. They can also provide flexibility for people relocating for work or saving toward homeownership.
Norris says lawmakers and builders should encourage built-to-rent communities and rental-friendly zoning to give North Carolina families more housing choices.
body: by Wadeyn Norris, State Chairman of the NC Federation of College Republicans In much of the state, fewer than 1% of for-sale homes are available at any given time — far below the 2–3% economists consider a healthy market. In the Triangle and Charlotte, where employers keep adding jobs faster than builders can add roofs, the math simply doesn't work for a growing share of families. Zoning reform and new construction are essential, and they take years to show results. In the meantime, North Carolina has a resource that's helping families right now: single-family rental homes. For a growing number of North Carolina families, a rented single-family home isn't a consolation prize — it's the smarter choice. It means a yard for the kids, a driveway, room to spread out, and access to the school district a family wants, all without a 20% down payment or a mortgage that locks them into one house for a decade. It means a young family relocating for a new job at one of the plants and employers investing in this state can move in within weeks, not months. And when the water heater breaks or the roof needs work, it's the landlord's problem, not a surprise bill that wrecks a family's budget. Single-family rentals also give families flexibility that ownership can't. A parent whose job moves them to Charlotte, a couple who wants to test out a neighborhood before committing, a family who needs more space after a second child arrives — all of them are better served by a rental market that includes single-family homes, not just apartments and condos. And for many renters, it's a stepping stone: a chance to build savings and credit history in a home that actually fits their life, on the way to owning one someday. As builders and lawmakers work to close North Carolina's housing gap, they should treat single-family rentals as part of the solution, not an afterthought. Expanding this segment of the market — through more built-to-rent communities and rental-friendly zoning — gives families real choices today while the state works to build its way out of a decades-in-the-making shortage. North Carolina families deserve options, and single-family rentals are one of the best ones we have.

hook: In much of the state, fewer than 1% of for-sale homes are available at any given time — far below the 2–3% economists consider a healthy market. In the Triangle and Charlotte, where employers keep adding jobs faster than builders can add roofs, the math simply doesn't work for a growing share of families.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: by Wadeyn Norris, State Chairman of the NC Federation of College Republicans In much of the state, fewer than 1% of for-sale homes are available at any given time — far below the 2–3% economists consider a healthy market. In the Triangle and Charlotte, where employers keep adding jobs faster than builders can add roofs, the math simply doesn't work for a growing share of families. Zoning reform and new construction are essential, and they take years to show results. In the meantime, North Carolina has a resource that's helping families right now: single-family rental homes. For a growing number of North Carolina families, a rented single-family home isn't a consolation prize — it's the smarter choice. It means a yard for the kids, a driveway, room to spread out, and access to the school district a family wants, all without a 20% down payment or a mortgage that locks them into one house for a decade. It means a young family relocating for a new job at one of the plants and employers investing in this state can move in within weeks, not months. And when the water heater breaks or the roof needs work, it's the landlord's problem, not a surprise bill that wrecks a family's budget. Single-family rentals also give families flexibility that ownership can't. A parent whose job moves them to Charlotte, a couple who wants to test out a neighborhood before committing, a family who needs more space after a second child arrives — all of them are better served by a rental market that includes single-family homes, not just apartments and condos. And for many renters, it's a stepping stone: a chance to build savings and credit history in a home that actually fits their life, on the way to owning one someday. As builders and lawmakers work to close North Carolina's housing gap, they should treat single-family rentals as part of the solution, not an afterthought. Expanding this segment of the market — through more built-to-rent communities and rental-friendly zoning — gives families real choices today while the state works to build its way out of a decades-in-the-making shortage. North Carolina families deserve options, and single-family rentals are one of the best ones we have.

Stein challenges federal shift on disability-rights guidance Gov. The guidance addresses the right of people with disabilities to receive services in integrated community settings when appropriate. Stein said the U.S. Department of Justice created uncertainty by announcing that it would no longer rely on its longstanding Olmstead guidance. The governors’ action presents a state-federal legal and policy dispute involving implementation of the Americans with Disabilities Act. headline: NC Labor Department reports record $889,640 recovered for workers
hook: North Carolina’s workplace-retaliation bureau secured a record $889,640 in settlements and other monetary relief for workers during state fiscal 2026.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: The money came from settlements and other relief obtained through state investigations of alleged workplace retaliation. RALEIGH — The N.C. Department of Labor says its workplace-retaliation bureau secured a record $889,640 in monetary relief for workers during the 2026 state fiscal year. The total is the highest annual recovery reported by the department’s Retaliatory Employment Discrimination Bureau, according to Labor Commissioner Luke Farley. The bureau investigates complaints filed under the Retaliatory Employment Discrimination Act, commonly known as REDA. The state law protects workers against retaliation for engaging in specified legally protected activities. Those activities include reporting workplace-safety concerns, filing workers’ compensation claims, initiating wage-and-hour complaints and exercising other rights recognized under state law. The $889,640 includes settlements and other financial relief produced through the bureau’s investigations, mediation and conciliation work. Depending on a case’s circumstances, relief can include lost wages, lost benefits and compensation for other economic losses. The department did not disclose how many cases produced the record total, identify the employers involved or provide a comparison with the previous fiscal year’s recovery. Those omissions limit the conclusions that can be drawn about whether complaints, enforcement activity or average recoveries increased. Farley said the recoveries represented relief for workers who exercised rights protected by law. “No worker should have to fear losing a job or paycheck for reporting an unsafe condition or exercising a right protected by law,” Farley said. Workers generally must submit a written REDA complaint within 180 days of the alleged retaliatory action. The department investigates the complaint and may pursue voluntary resolution through mediation or conciliation. REDA applies to retaliation connected to several state employment statutes rather than functioning as a general workplace-discrimination law. Protected conduct can include actions associated with occupational safety, wage-and-hour requirements and workers’ compensation. The recovery total reflects enforcement during the state fiscal year that ended June 30. Because the department released only an aggregate amount, the announcement does not establish how much individual workers received or whether the bureau found violations in every investigated complaint. It does, however, provide a statewide measure of monetary relief obtained through the agency’s retaliation-enforcement process. headline: State expands financial-oversight standards to larger local governments
hook: North Carolina will apply its financial-oversight standards more consistently to larger local governments, adding Cary, Greensboro, Rocky Mount and Zebulon to an updated assistance list.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: Cary, Greensboro, Rocky Mount and Zebulon are among the larger governments being added to a state assistance list based on fiscal 2025 audits. RALEIGH — North Carolina’s Local Government Commission is changing how it identifies local governments for additional financial oversight, applying its standards more consistently to larger cities and towns that previously may have been left off the state’s assistance list. Cary, Greensboro, Rocky Mount and Zebulon are among the larger governments being placed on the commission’s updated Unit Assistance List based on their fiscal 2025 audit reports, according to the Department of State Treasurer. The list identifies counties, municipalities and public authorities that may need additional monitoring or assistance from the state. Historically, larger governments that met the list’s financial criteria were not always included when commission staff determined those governments had enough personnel or other resources to correct the problems themselves. The commission said it is ending that practice and will apply the standards regardless of a government’s size. “Financial concerns should be taken seriously regardless of the size of the local government,” Treasurer Brad Briner said in announcing the change. Briner chairs the Local Government Commission, which is staffed by the Department of State Treasurer. The commission monitors the financial condition of more than 1,100 local government units and public authorities across North Carolina. It also reviews and approves most debt issued by those entities. Rocky Mount remains under enhanced state monitoring as commission staff work with local officials on identified financial and operational concerns. State officials cited that experience as an example of why larger governments may benefit from earlier intervention. The Unit Assistance List is also used to direct limited state oversight and assistance resources toward governments with identified problems. The state has not yet released the complete September 2026 list. The Department of State Treasurer said it will publish the list after every affected government has been notified. The previous list, based on fiscal 2024 audits and released in fall 2025, contained 146 counties, municipalities, utility authorities and districts. Placement on the list does not mean the Local Government Commission has assumed control of a government’s finances. It indicates that the unit has met one or more standards for additional review, monitoring or technical assistance. The change nevertheless broadens the practical reach of the state’s financial-oversight process by removing an informal distinction that sometimes kept larger governments off the published list. headline: Federal court blocks mandatory USPS ballot-mail rules for 2026 election
hook: A federal judge has blocked mandatory USPS ballot-envelope and voter-data requirements for the Nov. 3 election, granting relief sought by North Carolina and other states.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: The preliminary injunction prevents the Postal Service from enforcing new ballot-envelope and voter-data requirements as North Carolina begins mailing absentee ballots. RALEIGH — A federal judge has temporarily blocked the United States Postal Service from enforcing mandatory portions of a new ballot-mail rule during the Nov. 3 midterm election, granting relief sought by North Carolina and other states. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued the preliminary injunction Friday, the same day North Carolina’s county election boards began mailing absentee ballots to eligible voters who requested them. The ruling prohibits USPS from requiring state and local election officials to comply with new ballot-envelope design, approval and voter-data requirements before the Postal Service will handle their ballots. States may comply voluntarily when permitted under their own laws, but USPS cannot make compliance a condition of carrying election mail during the 2026 election. The new rule would have required election officials to submit ballot and return-envelope designs to USPS for approval. Officials also would have been required to upload voter information through a Postal Service portal before ballots could be mailed. Under the rule, USPS could decline to handle ballots when election officials had not obtained envelope approval, uploaded voter information or included required identifying barcodes. Talwani wrote that implementing the system fewer than 70 days before the election threatened to disenfranchise voters. The court found that state and local officials were already carrying out voter registration, ballot preparation, poll-worker training and other election responsibilities. The court also cited evidence that the required electronic portal was not operational and that printing redesigned ballot materials ordinarily could take four to 16 weeks. North Carolina was among 23 states and the District of Columbia that had challenged the underlying executive order directing USPS to develop the restrictions. After USPS issued its final rule in August, the states renewed their legal challenge. The judge found that the immediate implementation of the mandatory provisions threatened mail voters while the record contained no evidence of mail-voting fraud sufficient to justify the accelerated rollout. The injunction applies to the Nov. 3 election. It does not prohibit USPS from implementing the rule for later elections while the broader legal challenges proceed. North Carolina became the first state to begin sending absentee ballots for the 2026 general election. Under state election guidance, completed civilian absentee ballots must reach the voter’s county board of elections by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. headline: U.S. House censures North Carolina Rep. Chuck Edwards
hook: The U.S. House voted 413-2 to censure North Carolina Rep. Chuck Edwards following an investigation into his conduct toward two former staff members.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: The House voted 413-2 to formally reprimand Edwards after its Ethics Committee found that his conduct toward two former staff members violated chamber rules. WASHINGTON — The U.S. House voted 413-2 to censure North Carolina Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards, formally reprimanding him over conduct involving two young women who worked in his congressional office. The House approved the censure resolution Sept. 1 and required Edwards to present himself in the chamber well while the resolution was read. The action adopted the findings of a House Ethics Committee report issued in August. The bipartisan committee said Edwards engaged in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward the two staff members. According to the report, that conduct included repeated gifts, comments about their appearance and clothing, invitations to dinners and vacations, personal notes and other attempts to spend time with them. The committee said it found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or explicitly propositioned anyone working for him. It nevertheless concluded that his behavior would cause a reasonable observer to interpret it as sexual or romantic and that both women were placed in a difficult position because Edwards was their employer. The committee reported that it reviewed nearly 1,500 pages of documents and conducted 16 witness interviews, including an interview with Edwards. It concluded that his conduct failed to reflect creditably on the House and violated the spirit of chamber rules governing sexual harassment and unwanted advances. Edwards disputed important portions of the committee’s findings. In a response submitted by his attorneys, he argued that the committee’s process did not give him a sufficient opportunity to challenge the evidence and that its report failed to establish a violation of federal sexual-harassment law. The response said Edwards regretted that his behavior caused discomfort but maintained that gifts, messages and other interactions were not intended as unwanted romantic advances. His attorneys also argued that the committee gave insufficient weight to evidence that Edwards believed his relationships with the staff members were reciprocal friendships. The censure vote marks a final House action on the recommendation covered by NC Political News in August. Censure is a formal condemnation by the chamber but does not remove a representative from office or prevent the representative from voting. Edwards represents North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. He previously announced that he would not seek another term. headline: G20 ministers back Carolina Principles at Chapel Hill summit
hook: CHAPEL HILL - G20 ministers meeting in North Carolina backed the Carolina Principles, a framework calling for flexible technology policy, research investment and trusted deployment.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: CHAPEL HILL - G20 ministers meeting in North Carolina reached consensus on a technology-policy framework called the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, capping a two-day Innovation Ministerial hosted by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. The Sept. 1-2 gathering at the Carolina Inn brought government ministers together with executives from some of the world's largest technology companies. The White House said the resulting ministerial statement covers six areas: pro-innovation policy, technology-driven opportunity, technical workforce development, intellectual property policy for artificial intelligence, AI standards and industrial investment in supply chains. The Carolina Principles call for countries to invest in foundational research, strengthen pathways for commercializing new technology and enable trusted adoption and deployment. The ministerial also produced AI Prosperity Objectives and an AI Prosperity Compact aimed at technical workforce development and private-sector partnerships. Reuters reported that the joint statement generally favors using existing legal frameworks for AI and reserving new rules for problems not already covered by current law. China was among the countries that signed the statement. Copyright policy was a major point of discussion. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged G20 countries to build frameworks that protect creators while allowing AI companies to train models under fair-use principles. Reuters said he did not spell out how countries should determine fair use. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged officials to focus on real-world problems rather than theoretical harms when considering AI regulation. Other speakers included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. The White House said the ministerial included representatives from G20 members and invited participants spanning North America, Europe, Asia, South America, Africa and the Middle East. headline: Vertiv agrees to buy Raleigh power firm for up to $2.6 billion
hook: RALEIGH - Vertiv has agreed to acquire Raleigh-based UtilityInnovation Group for about $1.45 billion at closing, with up to $1.15 billion more tied to earnings targets.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: RALEIGH - Vertiv Holdings Co. has agreed to acquire Raleigh-based Utility Innovation Holdings Inc., which operates as UtilityInnovation Group, for about $1.45 billion in cash at closing, with up to $1.15 billion in additional payments tied to earnings targets. The transaction could reach about $2.6 billion if UtilityInnovation Group meets specified earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization targets over 12- and 24-month periods. Vertiv said the initial price represents about 13 times the company's expected 2027 EBITDA. UtilityInnovation Group develops microgrid controls, specialized switchgear and behind-the-meter power systems for data centers. Vertiv said the acquisition would add technology that coordinates utility power, onsite generation and energy storage, extending its infrastructure offerings toward the grid connection. Founded in 2020, UtilityInnovation Group is headquartered in Raleigh and has manufacturing operations in North Carolina and New Jersey. Its European headquarters is in Dublin, Ireland. Reuters reported that demand for microgrids and onsite power systems has grown as artificial intelligence workloads increase electricity needs and data center operators look for alternatives to constrained utility grids. Such systems can combine utility power, onsite generation and storage to improve reliability and shorten development timelines. Vertiv expects the transaction to add to adjusted earnings per share in the first year after completion. The agreement is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, and the companies expect it to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. headline: flyExclusive moves corporate headquarters to Raleigh
hook: RALEIGH - flyExclusive has moved its corporate headquarters from Kinston to Raleigh, bringing more than 120 employees and senior leaders to One North Hills.

body: RALEIGH - flyExclusive Inc. has moved its corporate headquarters from Kinston to One North Hills in Raleigh, bringing more than 120 employees and senior leaders, including Chairman and CEO Jim Segrave, to the new office. The publicly traded private aviation company opened the space after announcing its Raleigh expansion in January. At that time, flyExclusive said it had nearly 30 Raleigh employees, expected temporary space for about 50 employees by February and planned a permanent office accommodating roughly 125 people by June. The company said the Raleigh office was intended to help it recruit talent, improve collaboration and support growth. Segrave told Axios that the move is aimed in part at hiring for technology, sales, customer success and finance roles. Kinston remains a major operating center. flyExclusive said its maintenance, repair and overhaul work, including paint, interiors, avionics and maintenance, would stay at the North Carolina Global TransPark, along with maintenance leadership. In January, the company also said it was advancing a simulator training center and a 121,000-square-foot hangar project in Kinston and evaluating a second paint booth. Axios reported Sept. 3 that most maintenance and training staff remain in Kinston. Axios reported flyExclusive generated nearly $376 million in revenue last year and operates hundreds of flights worldwide each day. The company is using AI-driven systems to monitor sales, fuel use, maintenance turnaround and crew locations, and it plans to continue investing in its Contrails scheduling software. headline: Albemarle names Ragnar Udd as next CEO
hook: CHARLOTTE - Albemarle has named BHP executive Ragnar Udd as its next president and CEO, effective Feb. 1, 2027.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: CHARLOTTE - Albemarle Corp. has appointed BHP executive Ragnar "Rag" Udd president and chief executive officer, effective Feb. 1, 2027. He will also join Albemarle's board of directors. Chairman and CEO Kent Masters will move into the executive chairman role when Udd joins the company. Albemarle said Masters will serve as executive chairman through the company's 2027 annual meeting, after which the board will review his role annually as part of its director nomination process. Gerald Steiner will continue as lead independent director. Udd has more than 25 years of experience leading global resources businesses across Australia, Asia and North and South America. He is BHP's chief commercial officer and a member of its executive leadership team, with responsibility for global sales and marketing, procurement, maritime activities and commodities market strategy. His earlier BHP roles include president of the Americas, where he led the company's copper and potash businesses, as well as interim chief technology officer, BHP Mitsubishi Alliance asset president and vice president of logistics and infrastructure for Western Australia Iron Ore. Reuters reported that Udd, 54, is Canadian and plans to relocate to Albemarle's North Carolina headquarters in 2027. He succeeds Masters, who has led Albemarle since April 2020. The leadership change comes as the lithium producer navigates a volatile market. Reuters reported that lithium prices fell from record highs in 2023 after a surge in production created a supply glut, prompting producers to cut costs, delay projects and restructure operations. Prices have recovered in recent months and remain below their 2023 peaks. Sources Albemarle CEO succession announcement Reuters report on Albemarle CEO succession

headline: Partnership says UNCW, CFCC nursing capacity grew 77.5%
hook: A New Hanover County workforce partnership backed by a $22.3 million investment says nursing enrollment capacity at UNCW and Cape Fear Community College has grown 77.5% since 2023.
next_step: Review script and confirm story image before publishing.
body: WILMINGTON, N.C. - Nursing enrollment capacity at the University of North Carolina Wilmington and Cape Fear Community College has grown 77.5% since 2023, according to the New Hanover Healthcare Career Partnership, a regional workforce initiative backed by a $22.3 million investment from The Endowment. The partnership launched in 2024 and brings together UNCW, Cape Fear Community College, New Hanover County Schools and the Greater Wilmington Chamber of Commerce. Its work is designed to connect students with health care careers from middle school through employment while helping regional employers build a larger local talent pipeline. UNCW said the partnership's strategy includes early career exploration, expanded nursing education, student-success programs, employer engagement and workforce development. Grant-funded support also helps nursing students address barriers such as housing and child care so they can remain focused on classroom and clinical work. Jack C. Watson II, dean of UNCW's College of Health and Human Services, said the two colleges are working to educate more nurses and retain them in New Hanover County after graduation to help fill health care vacancies. Mary Ellen Naylor, dean of health sciences at Cape Fear Community College, said removing nonacademic barriers can help students complete their education and enter the workforce. The 77.5% figure refers to enrollment capacity. The sources do not report current enrollment totals, underlying seat totals or each college's share of the added capacity. The partnership's website describes the $22.3 million as support for the broader health care workforce initiative, which also includes K-12 pathways, student services and employer coordination. The partnership plans a public information session Sept. 22 at UNCW's Lumina Theater in the Fisher Student Center.
